summary: RedisTimeoutErrors are occurring in payment‑api despite low client pool usage and ample Redis CPU. Packet loss of ~12% was observed after a recent network change, and increasing the client pool size did not alleviate the issue, indicating the root cause is likely a network‑level degradation rather than Redis capacity.
likely_root_cause: Network path degradation introduced by the recent network configuration change, causing ~12% packet loss between payment‑api instances and the Redis cluster, leading to request timeouts despite sufficient Redis capacity and client pool headroom.

historical_incidents.memory_text: The payment-api service is experiencing Redis timeouts in production due to 12% packet loss following a network change.
Incident INC-58160236 occurred in the payment-api production service on 2026-09-28 due to Redis client pool exhaustion, causing checkout latency to reach 8 seconds.

The payment-api service is experiencing Redis timeouts in production despite having spare capacity. | When: 2026-09-29T01:31:24 | Redis timeouts returned following a network change, with 12% packet loss observed.

Incident INC-58160236 occurred in the payment-api production service due to Redis client pool exhaustion. | When: 2026-09-28 | Redis client pool reached 100/100 connections, causing checkout latency to reach 8 seconds.

The Redis client pool limit for the payment-api service was increased from 100 to 250 on 2026-09-28, and further increased to 300 on 2026-09-29, though the latter failed to resolve ongoing RedisTimeoutErrors.

memory_insights: Retained memory of a prior incident (INC-58160236) highlighted client‑pool exhaustion as a cause; this informs the current analysis that pool exhaustion must be explicitly ruled out.
The memory of the pool‑size increase attempt (source f0fc46fe-2e06-42f2-a921-46172fa65a05) confirms capacity is not the limiting factor.
recommended_actions: Temporarily revert the recent network configuration change (or apply a known‑good snapshot) on a single payment‑api instance to see if packet loss drops.
If rollback is not feasible, create an alternate routing rule or VPN tunnel that bypasses the changed segment for Redis traffic.
Adjust any newly introduced firewall or ACL rules to allow uninterrupted TCP traffic on the Redis port, then monitor for loss reduction.
investigation_steps: Run continuous ping/traceroute from payment‑api pods to Redis nodes to quantify loss and latency trends.
Collect interface statistics (errors, drops, retransmits) on the network devices handling traffic to Redis.
Review change‑control logs for the network change applied shortly before the incident (e.g., firewall rule, routing update, MTU change).
Check Redis server logs for any network‑related warnings or connection resets.
If available, capture a short tcpdump on a payment‑api host targeting Redis to inspect retransmissions.
next_steps: Run continuous ping/traceroute from payment‑api pods to Redis nodes to quantify loss and latency trends.
risk_notes: Reverting network changes may temporarily affect other services that rely on the same path; perform the rollback on a single instance first and monitor impact. Adding an alternate route is low‑risk but requires coordination with networking. All actions are reversible and do not involve restarting Redis or the payment‑api service.
evidence_assessment: Observed packet loss (12%) and low pool utilization (28%) directly contradict a pool‑exhaustion hypothesis. The failed pool‑size increase confirms capacity is not the limiting factor. Historical incidents of pool exhaustion are not consistent with current metrics.
disconfirming_checks: Verify Redis server CPU and memory remain within normal ranges (no spikes).
Confirm client pool metrics show no saturation (connections <30% of limit).
Check that Redis latency metrics (if any) are low (<5 ms) despite packet loss.
Ensure no recent Redis configuration changes (e.g., maxclients) were applied.
verification_steps: Re‑measure packet loss after the network rollback; target <2% sustained loss.
Observe RedisTimeoutError rate for at least 5 minutes; expect zero occurrences.
Confirm payment‑api request latency returns to baseline levels.
Document that the network change has been either rolled back or safely replaced.
